column4: The section’s central scene is stated here: pure provision is given, transgression brings “My wrath” to settle upon them, and the one it reaches falls; it makes the two possible descents concrete.
Immediately after 20:81’s fall under wrath, this ayah gives the other ending: repentance, faith, righteous action, and then guidance, exactly the section’s forgiveness-versus-lost-way contrast.
Moses returns غضبان, visibly angry and grieved, and asks whether they wanted wrath from their Lord to settle upon them; it joins bodily anger to the divine wrath-upon-a-people scene.
The preceding ayah recalls rescue from the enemy and manna and quails sent down to Israel, supplying the bestowed provision whose abuse 20:81 sets against divine wrath.
Moses returns غضبان أسفا after the calf; his rebuke and physical seizure of Aaron stage the section’s secondary, bodily sense of anger beside the people’s later divine punishment.
For the calf-makers, wrath from their Lord and humiliation will reach them. It is the section’s explicit pairing of descending anger with abasement, opposed to chosen lowliness.
Manna and quails are sent down over Israel and they are told to eat the good provision; this is the provision side of the same Israel scene that later turns to wrath when it is abused.
After the command of 2:57–58 is altered, a punishment is sent down from heaven on the wrongdoers. It reverses the earlier food descending upon them.
This parallel Israel account explicitly has cloud shade and manna and quails over them, a concrete image of good provision placed upon a people.
When the wrongdoers replace the commanded word, a punishment is sent down upon them from heaven; it supplies the adverse counterpart to 7:160’s descending provision.
Israel rejects the given food, and the result is humiliation, poverty, and return with wrath from God. It tightly joins provision, ingratitude, abasement, and wrath.
Those who resent that God sends down His bounty return with wrath upon wrath. The ayah directly connects a descending divine gift with the wrath their refusal brings back.
Humiliation and poverty are imposed on them, and they return with wrath from God. This makes the section’s wrath-to-lowliness relation visible in public condition.
God is angry with, curses, and prepares grave punishment for the deliberate murderer. Its direct “God was angry with him” supplies the active divine side left passive in 1:7.
Those cursed and made objects of God’s anger are also described as farther astray from the level path; it explicitly joins wrath and loss of the way.
Their deeds have brought God’s displeasure upon them, so they remain in punishment. This is the سخط counterpart to the section’s rida/anger opposition.
Hud tells his people that defilement and wrath from their Lord have fallen upon them; the verb of falling makes wrath an event over a community.
Those who open their breasts to disbelief have wrath from God upon them. It is another direct “upon them” judgment matching the passive group in 1:7.
The evil-thinkers have the evil turn upon them, and God is angry with and curses them. The ayah gives a named agent and a contrary destiny to the divinely pleased believers nearby.
The condemned group is identified as people with whom God is angry; it clarifies how an angry-upon people can become a moral association and allegiance.
Believers are told not to ally themselves with a people against whom God is angry. The contrast makes the 1:7 group a boundary for communal direction.
It asks whether one who follows God’s رضوان can be like one who returns with His سخط. This is the section’s rida-versus-anger movement stated as two opposed courses.
On the day religion is completed, God completes His نعمة upon the community and is pleased with Islam for them; favor and divine approval arrive together.
God guides those who follow His رضوان along paths of peace and out of darkness. It makes following divine pleasure a route, illuminating the blessed people’s way.
On the decisive day, God is pleased with the truthful and they are pleased with Him. Reciprocal rida supplies the fulfilled opposite of wrath.
The Lord gives believers good news of mercy, رضوان, and enduring gardens of نعيم. It gathers mercy, pleasure, and the نعيم family on the favorable side.
Gardens and dwellings culminate in رضوان from God, called greater still. It distinguishes divine pleasure from merely received comforts.
The first emigrants, helpers, and their followers receive the reciprocal formula: God is pleased with them and they with Him. It is a named community on the rida side.
Moses says he hastened to his Lord so that He would be pleased. Within the calf narrative, his movement toward rida counterpoints the people’s choice of wrath.
God does not approve disbelief for His servants but approves gratitude. It makes acceptance and rejection of a response the rida-side boundary to anger.
They follow what angers God and hate what pleases Him, ruining their works. The ayah places the two opposed directions in one sentence.
God is pleased with the believers at the pledge, knows what is in their hearts, and sends down tranquility on them. It is rida visibly enacted on a gathered people.
God is pleased with His party and they with Him. This reciprocal community is the positive social counterpart to 58:14’s people of divine anger.
The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord راضية مرضية, both pleased and pleasing. It gives rida the calm, inward face that answers anger.
The final garden reward is sealed by “God is pleased with them and they with Him,” the completed communal alternative to the angry-upon group.
After danger, the believers return with bounty and favor, untouched by harm, because they followed God’s رضوان; it joins received grace to a chosen direction.

Those who obey God and the Messenger are with those upon whom God has bestowed favor—prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous—and they are excellent companions. It names the blessed group and its shared road.

The prophets and chosen people are explicitly those upon whom God bestowed favor and guided; when recitation reaches them, they fall in prostration and weeping. It gives the favored group a bodily response.
God completes His نعمة upon the community so that they may be guided. It directly binds completed favor to the guidance ending contrasted with wrath and falling.
Moses tells Israel to remember God’s favor upon them—prophets, kings, and gifts given to no other peoples—before their later refusal and punishment.
Solomon asks to be enabled to thank the نعمة God bestowed upon him and his parents and to do what God approves. It links favor, gratitude, and pleasing conduct.
God has lavished manifest and hidden نعمة upon people. Its visible/hidden distribution expands the section’s image of what is placed upon a person.
The mature child prays to thank the نعمة bestowed on him and his parents and asks to act righteously. It turns received favor into a grateful, approved response.
On the day some faces whiten and others blacken, the darkened faces are confronted with disbelief and punishment. It renders the section’s two groups as two opposite faces.
The whitened faces are in God’s mercy forever. This supplies the favorable face missing from 3:106’s warning.
Those who do good receive the best and more; no dust or humiliation covers their faces. It directly reverses the section’s image of something dark settling over a face.
Wrongdoers’ faces are covered by humiliation, as though dark pieces of night covered them. It is a close visual parallel to faces overlaid by dust and darkness.
Some faces on that day are radiant. The ayah gives a concise eschatological version of the softened, favored face.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord; their gaze identifies the source of the favorable countenance in 75:22.
Other faces are باسرة, grim and contracted, furnishing the facial reverse of 75:22’s radiance.
The grim faces expect a crushing calamity. It explains the judgment-bearing expression of 75:24.
God protects them from that day’s evil and gives them نضرة and joy. This connects a day’s rescue to the fresh brightness later recognized in faces of نعيم.

When a daughter is announced, a man’s face becomes dark while he is inwardly constricted. It is a concrete Qur’anic facial trace of a destructive emotional stance, without equating it to divine wrath.
When the later promise comes, servants are sent to afflict their faces and enter the sanctuary. The face becomes the exposed surface of historical punishment.
Hostility to clear recitation is recognized in disbelievers’ faces before they attack the reciters. It gives a present-world face that bears a hostile inner response.
Fire scorches their faces and leaves them كالحون, grim and distorted. It makes the adverse face more bodily than the dust-and-darkness image.
At death, angels strike the disbelievers’ faces and backs while announcing the burning punishment. The face is directly the surface receiving the consequence.
Fire covers their faces on the day of judgment. It intensifies the section’s “upon the face” image into a punitive covering.
The desperate are given a drink that burns faces, called بئس الشراب. Its explicit “wretched” judgment opposes the section’s نعم/بئس and face-of-favor contrast.
Disbelievers will be unable to keep the Fire from their faces or backs. It states a face directly exposed to the punishment they denied.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell have the worst place and are farthest from the way. It joins a debased face-bearing journey to being lost from the path.
Those who bring evil are thrown face-first into the Fire. The face becomes the point of the reversal that answers the radiant and prostrate face.
Their faces are turned over in the Fire as they wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger. The ayah gives a face-bound consequence of taking the wrong direction.
On the Day of Resurrection, the liars’ faces are blackened. It repeats the darkened-face side of the final division.
The believers’ mark is in their faces from prostration. It offers a present bodily sign of the group with whom God is pleased, rather than an anger-marked countenance.
Their eyes are humbled and humiliation covers them when they are called to prostration. It links a lowered gaze and facial shame to refusal of worship.
With humbled eyes and humiliation covering them, they emerge toward the promised day. It repeats the face-and-humiliation scene as a day’s public condition.
Moses is returned to his mother so that her eye may be cool and she not grieve. It directly realizes the source dictionary’s “eye’s blessing” as calm sight after rescue.
Mary is told to eat, drink, and cool her eye. Provision and an eye made calm appear together, a concrete favorable face-image.
Servants of the Merciful ask for spouses and offspring who are a coolness of the eyes. It extends the source’s “eye’s blessing” from relief to a hoped-for household.
Pharaoh’s wife calls the infant Moses a coolness of the eye for her and Pharaoh. The phrase gives the positive eye-image even in a household soon divided by response to him.
Moses is returned to his mother so that her eye may be cool and she not grieve. It repeats the rescued-eye scene with the mother’s relief as its own outcome.
What is hidden for the righteous includes coolnesses of the eyes as recompense. The unseen reward makes the calm eye a final rather than merely temporary favor.
God sends down His tranquility upon the Messenger and believers, sends unseen forces, and punishes disbelievers. It stages calm descending on one side and punishment on the other.
God sends down tranquility into believers’ hearts so that faith increases. This inward cooling is a close counterpart to the section’s softened face and cool eye.
While disbelievers carry heated zeal, God sends down His tranquility on the Messenger and believers. It is an explicit cooling-versus-heated-hostility contrast.
Angels descend upon the steadfast with “do not fear or grieve” and good news of the Garden. A favorable descent replaces the terror associated with judgment.
The disciples ask for a table to be sent down upon them as a sign, festival, and provision. It makes a beneficent thing descending upon a community explicit.
God says He will send the table down, but disbelief after it will bring unequalled punishment. The same descent becomes a boundary between received favor and wrathful consequence.
Moses is commanded to remind his people of the “days of God,” the phrase the section glosses as days of punishment and forgiveness or favors.
Moses’ reminder begins with rescue from Pharaoh’s severe torture. It supplies the salvation-versus-affliction content of the days named in 14:5.
Believers are told to forgive those who do not hope for the days of God, when each people will be repaid. It preserves the section’s day-language as a horizon of differentiated recompense.
God does not change a favor He bestowed on a people until they change themselves. It explains how a bestowed نعمة can be forfeited before punishment comes.
Those who exchange God’s نعمة for disbelief make their people dwell in the home of ruin. It is an exact reversal of given favor into a ruinous destination.
A secure, well-provided town denies God’s favors, so God makes it taste the garment of hunger and fear. Favor reverses into an enveloping bodily condition.
Eat the lawful, good provision God has given and thank His نعمة. In its local context, gratitude is the alternative to 16:112’s reversal of favor.
When the human is honored and given ease, he calls it his Lord’s honoring. The ayah uses نعمه to test the easy equation of provision with settled approval.
When provision is measured out, he calls it humiliation; together with 89:15 it corrects reading every ease as favor and every restriction as wrath.
The tranquil soul begins the return scene completed in 89:28. Its calm interior forms the fitting condition for reciprocal pleasure.
Israel is told to remember God’s نعمة that He bestowed upon them and to fulfill their covenant. It repeats the blessed-upon formula as a call to response.
The same command recalls the favor bestowed upon Israel and their distinction among peoples. It shows that received favor entails a historical responsibility.
Again Israel is reminded of the favor bestowed upon them. Its repetition gives the favor a communal and remembered, rather than private, form.
Purification and completion of God’s نعمة are joined so that the community may be grateful. It connects favor to a cleansed, responsive condition.
Believers are told to remember God’s favor upon them and His covenant. Like 2:40, it treats grace as a relation calling for fidelity.
God’s favor consists in restraining hostile hands from the believers. It shows نعمة as protection from an attack rather than only material provision.
Jesus is told to remember God’s favors upon him and his mother. It gives a named recipient of divine favor, paralleling the named favored people of 4:69 and 19:58.
Joseph’s dream is interpreted as election, teaching, and completion of God’s favor upon him and Jacob’s family. Favor here unfolds as guidance through a lineage.
Whoever exchanges God’s نعمة after it has come faces severe punishment. It gives the moral pivot between a received grace and its adverse sequel.
God’s favor turns former enemies into brothers and saves them from a brink of Fire. It makes favor a rescue that changes a community’s condition.
Every نعمة people possess comes from God, and distress drives them back to Him. It names God as the source of the favorable side before human response divides.
They recognize God’s نعمة and then deny it. This defines ingratitude as a refusal of an already known favor, preparing the reversals in the surrounding passage.
When God bestows favor on the human, he turns away; when harm touches him, he despairs. It maps the unstable response to grace that the Israel provision scenes warn against.
After calling on God in hardship, a person forgets when granted a نعمة from Him. The ayah traces how relief can fail to become gratitude.
When We bestow favor on the human, he turns aside; when evil touches him, his prayer becomes expansive. It repeats the embodied turning-away response to favor.
Believers are told to remember God’s favor when armies came: He sent wind and unseen forces against the attackers. Protection upon one group is adversity upon the other.
“Remember God’s favor upon you” is immediately tied to God alone providing provision from heaven and earth. It grounds every received نعمة in a single giver.
Riders are told to remember their Lord’s نعمة when settled upon mounts. The verse makes gratitude arise precisely when the body is made securely placed.
The Messenger is told to speak of his Lord’s نعمة. It connects the section’s hamd-side approval to voicing received favor.
After wrongdoers are cut off, the response is “praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.” It places hamd beside a judgment that exposes the opposite of approval.
The final call of the garden’s people is praise to God, Lord of the worlds. It supplies a blessed community whose speech answers the opening hamd.
David and Solomon praise God for favoring them over many believing servants. Praise is here the explicit reception of a distinguishing divine gift.
Garden-dwellers praise God for removing grief from them. It joins hamd to the relieved, favorable bodily condition opposed to the grief and humiliation of judgment.
The inheritors of the Garden praise God for fulfilling His promise. Their hamd belongs to the completed favorable destiny, not merely an abstract formula.
At revelation, fearful skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften. It is a nonlexical parallel to the source dictionary’s softening sense of نعمة, with the bodily change tied to God’s word.
The believers are those who, when they become angry, forgive. It turns the source’s anger-as-vengeful impulse toward its opposite outcome.
The God-conscious restrain rage and pardon people. This is the practical reversal of the section’s description of anger as a surge toward retaliation.
The people God brings are humble toward believers and strong toward disbelievers. Their chosen humility illuminates the contrast with the imposed humiliation that accompanies wrath in 7:152.
A person gives himself seeking God’s pleasure. It makes pursuit of رضوان an actual direction of life, answering the return with divine displeasure.
Spending is done seeking God’s pleasure and inner firmness. The verse gives rida a concrete ethical motive rather than a mere final verdict.
For the God-conscious, gardens and purified spouses are joined by رضوان from God. It locates divine pleasure at the heart of the favorable final condition.
Secret counsel for charity, kindness, or reconciliation can be done seeking God’s pleasure. It specifies a social route toward rida rather than anger.
Pilgrims seek bounty from their Lord and His pleasure. The road-and-seeking setting strengthens the section’s picture of rida as a course one follows.
Some are pleased only when given from charity and become resentful when withheld. It contrasts contingent human satisfaction with the stable divine rida in the section.
Even if believers are pleased with the hypocrites, God is not pleased with the defiantly corrupt. The ayah separates human acceptance from divine approval.
A foundation built on God-consciousness and His pleasure is contrasted with one collapsing from a crumbling brink into Fire. It makes rida a stable ground against a fall.
The oppressed will be admitted to an entrance with which they are pleased. It gives human rida as the received, favorable side of divine vindication.
The one who gives seeking the face of his highest Lord will soon be pleased. It turns selfless pursuit of God into a promised state of rida.
The Lord will give the Messenger until he is pleased. It links gift and rida in a compact personal form.
After 19:58’s favored, guided worshippers, successors neglect prayer and follow desire, meeting ghayy. It is the local reversal from guided favor to being lost.
Repentance, faith, and righteous deeds lead into the Garden after 19:59’s ghayy. It repeats the section’s route from failure through forgiveness to guidance.
Whoever follows God’s guidance will neither go astray nor suffer. It compresses the guided ending that 20:82 sets against falling under wrath.
Guidance opens the breast to Islam, while misguidance makes it tight and constricted. Its bodily contrast parallels the section’s two inward states made visible on faces.
When they hear what was sent down to the Messenger, their eyes overflow with tears because they recognize truth. It is a specific favorable, receptive mark in the eyes.
The opening verb says he frowned. Because the source explicitly develops a frowning face as a secondary sense of anger, this is a literal facial parallel without assigning the same motive.
The rejecter frowns and scowls before turning away in pride. It gives the source’s frowning facial image an explicit scene of hostile refusal.
Jonah departs in anger, then calls from darkness and is rescued. His story gives human anger a movement toward confession and deliverance rather than vengeance.
When Moses’ anger subsides, he takes the tablets whose guidance and mercy are for those who fear their Lord. The link is indirect, but it completes 7:150’s bodily anger with a return to guidance.
Israel is told to eat freely, enter humbly, and ask forgiveness so that sins will be forgiven and goodness increased. It supplies the responsive alternative just before 7:162’s punishment.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell. It supplies the judged group whose facial scorching is described concretely in 23:104.
Their humbled eyes accompany emergence from graves toward the caller. This is a specific eschatological gaze of abasement, though it does not itself name wrath.
On the quaking day, eyes are lowered in humility. It is a parallel final-day facial condition to the humiliated faces developed in the section.
Jacob’s eyes turn white from grief while he suppresses sorrow. This is an indirect parallel: emotion leaves a visible bodily trace around the eyes, though the emotion is not anger.
